metadata.title: IELTS 8.0 Academic Vocabulary Collection
metadata.source: Anki 2.1 Collection (IELTS 8.0) + AWL Sublists 1-10 + C1/C2 Academic Lexicon

realms.name: The Scholastic Citadel
realms.desc: Master academic vocabulary from the halls of learning.

words.definition: the subjects that are studied in a school, college or course
words.example: Many argue that the school curriculum should include practical life skills such as managing money.

words.definition: learning by repeating information until you remember it, rather than understanding it
words.example: Exam-driven systems are often criticised for encouraging rote learning at the expense of critical thinking.

words.definition: the money paid for being taught, especially at a college or university
words.example: Some governments have abolished tuition fees in order to widen access to higher education.

words.definition: connected with the skills and knowledge needed for a particular job
words.example: Vocational courses can equip young people with the skills that employers actually need.

words.definition: the process of continuing to learn new skills and knowledge throughout adult life
words.example: Rapid technological change has made lifelong learning essential for most workers.

words.definition: that must be done because of a rule or law
words.example: Physical education should remain a compulsory subject in secondary schools.

words.definition: the ability to read and write
words.example: Improving adult literacy can transform the economic prospects of rural communities.

words.definition: how well a student does in their studies
words.example: There is growing evidence that sleep has a direct impact on academic performance.

words.definition: the ability to analyse information objectively and make a reasoned judgement
words.example: Debate clubs help students develop critical thinking and confidence.

words.definition: done in addition to the normal course of study
words.example: Extracurricular activities such as sport and music teach children teamwork.

words.definition: the practice of training people to obey rules and control their behaviour
words.example: Teachers often struggle to maintain discipline in overcrowded classrooms.

words.meaning: giáo dục đại học, sau phổ thông
words.definition: education at university or college level
words.example: Access to tertiary education should depend on ability rather than wealth.

words.definition: money given to a student to help pay for their education
words.example: She won a full scholarship to study engineering abroad.

words.definition: a way of studying from home, usually online, without attending classes in person
words.example: Distance learning gives working adults the flexibility to study at their own pace.

words.definition: the percentage of students who leave school or a course before finishing
words.example: Free school meals have helped to reduce the dropout rate in poorer areas.

words.definition: including students of different levels of ability
words.example: Teaching mixed-ability classes requires careful planning.

words.definition: the process of judging how well someone has learned something
words.example: Continuous assessment may give a fairer picture of a student's ability than a single exam.

words.definition: the methods and theory of teaching
words.example: Many teacher-training programmes now emphasise student-centred pedagogy.

words.definition: having a wide range of skills, interests and experience
words.example: Schools should aim to produce well-rounded individuals, not just high scorers.

words.definition: influence from people of your own age to behave like them
words.example: Teenagers often succumb to peer pressure to fit in with their classmates.

words.definition: to study very hard for a short time before an exam
words.example: Students who cram the night before an exam rarely retain the information.

words.definition: to officially join a course or school
words.example: More adults are enrolling on part-time courses to update their skills.

words.definition: to gain knowledge or a skill
words.example: Young children acquire languages more easily than adults.

words.definition: a clear understanding of something; to understand something completely
words.example: A firm grasp of basic maths is essential for everyday life.

words.definition: a test given and scored in the same way for all students
words.example: Critics argue that standardised tests measure memory rather than intelligence.

words.meaning: chế độ trọng dụng nhân tài
words.definition: a system in which people succeed because of ability rather than wealth or class
words.example: Scholarships help make higher education more of a meritocracy.

words.meaning: học tập dựa trên khám phá
words.definition: learning in which students investigate questions themselves
words.example: Inquiry-based learning encourages pupils to ask their own questions.

words.meaning: chương trình học nghề (vừa học vừa làm)
words.definition: a period of on-the-job training with a skilled worker
words.example: Apprenticeships allow young people to earn while they learn.

words.meaning: khoảng cách thành tích học tập
words.definition: the difference in results between groups of students
words.example: Tutoring programmes aim to close the attainment gap between rich and poor pupils.

words.definition: a family situation with little money or opportunity
words.example: Students from disadvantaged backgrounds are less likely to attend university.

words.definition: money borrowed to pay for university study
words.example: Many graduates spend years repaying their student loans.

words.meaning: khả năng có việc làm của sinh viên tốt nghiệp
words.definition: the degree to which graduates have the skills employers want
words.example: Work placements can improve graduate employability.

words.definition: involving practical experience rather than theory
words.example: Science is best taught through hands-on experiments.

words.definition: based on ideas rather than real, physical things
words.example: Young children find abstract concepts such as time difficult.

words.meaning: tính tự chủ của người học
words.definition: students' ability to take control of their own learning
words.example: Online courses demand a high degree of learner autonomy.

words.definition: the desire to do something because it is interesting or satisfying in itself
words.example: Excessive rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation.

words.definition: coming from outside, such as rewards or punishments
words.example: Prizes are an extrinsic motivator whose effect may not last.

words.definition: honesty in academic work, without cheating or copying
words.example: AI writing tools pose new challenges to academic integrity.

words.definition: presenting someone else's work as your own
words.example: Universities use software to detect plagiarism.

words.definition: to change a system completely in order to improve it
words.example: The government plans to overhaul the national curriculum.

words.definition: the list of topics covered in a course
words.example: Teachers struggle to cover the entire syllabus before exams.

words.meaning: bài tập tính điểm trong khóa học
words.definition: work done during a course that counts towards the final grade
words.example: Coursework rewards steady effort rather than exam technique.

words.definition: very careful and demanding high standards
words.example: Medical students undergo rigorous training.

words.definition: having exceptional intellectual ability
words.example: Special programmes can stretch academically gifted pupils.

words.definition: dividing students into classes according to ability
words.example: Critics argue that streaming labels children too early.

words.meaning: lấy giáo viên làm trung tâm
words.definition: where the teacher talks and students mainly listen
words.example: Teacher-centred lessons can leave students passive.

words.meaning: lấy người học làm trung tâm
words.definition: focused on students' needs and active participation
words.example: Student-centred learning encourages discussion and collaboration.

words.definition: educating children at home instead of at school
words.example: Some parents opt for home-schooling to tailor lessons to their child.

words.meaning: trường chỉ dành cho một giới
words.definition: a school for only boys or only girls
words.example: Some studies suggest that girls perform better in single-sex schools.

words.definition: teaching boys and girls together
words.example: Co-educational schools reflect the mixed nature of society.

words.definition: extra lessons that families pay for privately
words.example: Private tuition is extremely common in many Asian countries.

words.definition: focused mainly on passing examinations
words.example: An exam-oriented system may discourage creativity.

words.definition: the growth of a child's ability to think and understand
words.example: Reading aloud supports young children's cognitive development.

words.definition: education for children before they start primary school
words.example: Investment in early childhood education yields long-term benefits.

words.definition: the ability to understand and work with numbers
words.example: Basic numeracy is essential for managing personal finances.

words.definition: skills that are useful in many different jobs
words.example: Team projects build transferable skills such as communication.

words.definition: personal skills such as communication and teamwork
words.example: Employers complain that many graduates lack soft skills.

words.definition: combining two or more academic subjects
words.example: Climate studies require an interdisciplinary approach.

words.definition: an experienced person who advises a less experienced one
words.example: Mentoring schemes pair new teachers with experienced colleagues.

words.definition: a natural ability to do something
words.example: She showed an early aptitude for languages.

words.definition: existing from birth
words.example: Some people believe intelligence is largely innate.

words.definition: to help something develop; the care given to a child
words.example: Schools should nurture creativity, not merely test it.

words.meaning: thúc đẩy, khuyến khích phát triển
words.definition: to encourage something to develop
words.example: Group projects foster cooperation between students.

words.definition: to prevent something from developing
words.example: Overly strict rules can stifle students' creativity.

words.definition: to gradually make someone have a quality or feeling
words.example: Parents try to instil good habits in their children.

words.definition: to pass on knowledge or skills
words.example: A good teacher imparts knowledge in an engaging way.

words.definition: eager to learn and ask questions
words.example: Inquisitive children ask endless questions about the world.

words.definition: careful to do work well and thoroughly
words.example: Conscientious students rarely miss deadlines.

words.definition: showing care and steady effort
words.example: Diligent revision is more effective than last-minute study.

words.definition: to perform less well than your ability suggests
words.example: Bright pupils may underachieve if they are not challenged.

words.definition: staying away from school without permission
words.example: Truancy is often linked to problems at home.

words.definition: to officially make someone leave a school
words.example: He was expelled for repeated bullying.

words.definition: repeatedly hurting or frightening a weaker person
words.example: Schools must have clear anti-bullying policies.

words.meaning: học sinh vừa rời ghế phổ thông
words.definition: a young person who has just finished school
words.example: Many school leavers now choose apprenticeships over university.

words.meaning: năm nghỉ trước khi vào đại học
words.definition: a year off between school and university
collocations: defer entry for a gap year
words.example: A gap year can help students mature before university.

words.meaning: sau đại học; học viên sau đại học
words.definition: relating to study after a first degree
words.example: Postgraduate degrees are increasingly required for research posts.

words.definition: a university student studying for a first degree
words.example: Undergraduates often share accommodation in their first year.

words.definition: a department of a university; its academic staff
words.example: Faculty members are expected to publish research.

words.definition: a long piece of writing for a degree; a main argument
words.example: She is writing her thesis on urban migration.

words.definition: official approval that a course meets required standards
words.example: The course has gained international accreditation.

words.definition: respected and admired
words.example: Graduates of prestigious universities often earn higher salaries.

words.definition: a situation in which academics are cut off from ordinary life
collocations: step out of the ivory tower
words.example: Universities are sometimes criticised as ivory towers.

words.meaning: trình độ học vấn đạt được
words.definition: the highest level of education someone has completed
words.example: Educational attainment strongly predicts lifetime earnings.

words.definition: the inability to read and write
words.example: Adult education programmes aim to eradicate illiteracy.

words.meaning: học kết hợp (trực tuyến + trực tiếp)
words.definition: combining online study with face-to-face teaching
words.example: Blended learning combines the flexibility of online study with classroom support.

words.definition: a model where students study content at home and practise in class
words.example: In a flipped classroom, lectures are watched at home.

words.meaning: khóa học trực tuyến đại trà
words.definition: a free online course open to anyone (massive open online course)
words.example: MOOCs give millions of people access to university-level teaching.

words.definition: qualifications that show you are suitable for something
words.example: Employers increasingly look beyond academic credentials.

words.definition: an economy based on information and skills rather than manufacturing
words.example: Education is crucial to competing in the knowledge economy.

words.definition: to give someone the skills they need
words.example: Schools should equip students with practical life skills.

words.definition: to develop a skill, quality or interest
words.example: Libraries help children cultivate a love of reading.

words.definition: to make something wider or more varied
words.example: Studying abroad broadens students' horizons.

words.definition: having a lot of knowledge about a subject
words.example: Education produces well-informed citizens who can judge policies.

words.definition: to repeat information without understanding it
words.example: Examinations that merely reward students who regurgitate memorised facts fail to assess genuine understanding.

words.definition: the tendency for grades to rise without a real rise in standards
words.example: Grade inflation makes it harder for employers to compare candidates.

words.definition: a list ranking schools or universities by performance
words.example: Schools may focus on exam results to climb league tables.

words.meaning: sự chăm sóc tinh thần học sinh
words.definition: support for students' personal and emotional well-being
words.example: Good pastoral care helps students cope with stress.

words.meaning: nhu cầu giáo dục đặc biệt
words.definition: learning difficulties or disabilities that require extra support
words.example: Teachers need training to support pupils with special educational needs.

words.definition: teaching students of all abilities and backgrounds together
words.example: Inclusive education allows disabled children to learn alongside their peers.

words.definition: practical training for a particular job
words.example: Vocational training can reduce youth unemployment.

words.meaning: mang tính giáo huấn, thuyết giảng một chiều
words.definition: Intended to teach, especially in an overly moralising or rigid teacher-led manner.
words.example: Modern universities are gradually moving away from purely didactic lectures toward collaborative problem-solving workshops.

words.meaning: người tự học không qua đào tạo chính quy
words.definition: A self-taught person who acquires advanced knowledge or skills without formal schooling.
words.example: With open-access repositories proliferating online, a disciplined autodidact can now master complex disciplines independently.

words.meaning: thuộc về học thuật, trường lớp
words.definition: Relating to schools, academic study, and formal intellectual achievement.
words.example: Excessive emphasis on scholastic rankings often pressures secondary schools into narrowing their arts programmes.

words.meaning: uyên bác, thông thái sâu rộng
words.definition: Having or showing deep, extensive knowledge gained through serious study and reading.
words.example: The keynote speaker delivered an erudite critique of how standardised testing narrows intellectual exploration.

words.meaning: chính thức nhập học vào trường đại học
words.definition: To be formally admitted to study at a university or college after meeting entrance criteria.
words.example: Targeted outreach initiatives have enabled far more first-generation students to matriculate at prestigious institutions.

words.meaning: thuộc hoạt động bổ trợ gắn liền với chương trình học
words.definition: Complementing and directly reinforcing the formal academic curriculum rather than remaining separate from it.
words.example: Debating societies and laboratory clubs offer valuable co-curricular experiences that sharpen analytical reasoning.

words.meaning: bổ trợ, phụ đạo để khắc phục lỗ hổng kiến thức
words.definition: Designed to help students who are struggling to reach the expected academic standard.
words.example: Early diagnostic screening allows schools to provide targeted remedial support before minor literacy gaps widen.

words.meaning: đánh giá quá trình trong học tập
words.definition: Ongoing evaluation during a course used to monitor comprehension and adapt teaching methods accordingly.
words.example: Unlike high-stakes final examinations, formative assessment gives teachers timely insight into conceptual misunderstandings.

words.meaning: đánh giá tổng kết cuối kỳ hoặc cuối khóa
words.definition: Formal evaluation conducted at the end of an instructional period to measure overall mastery against benchmarks.
words.example: Critics argue that relying exclusively on summative assessment encourages cramming rather than durable understanding.

words.meaning: tính chặt chẽ và chuẩn mực nghiêm ngặt trong học thuật
words.definition: The high standard of thoroughness, intellectual challenge, and precision expected in scholarly work.
words.example: Expanding university access must not come at the expense of maintaining academic rigour across degree programmes.

words.meaning: siêu nhận thức (khả năng nhận biết và điều chỉnh cách tư duy của bản thân)
words.definition: Awareness and deliberate regulation of one's own thinking and learning processes.
words.example: Teaching adolescents strategies for metacognition significantly improves their ability to plan essays and self-correct errors.

words.meaning: giàn giáo sư phạm (hỗ trợ có định hướng và giảm dần theo tiến bộ người học)
words.definition: Temporary instructional support provided by educators and gradually withdrawn as learners gain independence.
words.example: Effective scaffolding enables novice writers to construct coherent arguments before tackling complex essays unassisted.

words.meaning: giảng dạy phân hóa theo năng lực từng học sinh
words.definition: A teaching framework that tailors content, pacing, and tasks to accommodate diverse student abilities.
words.example: In overcrowded classrooms, implementing differentiated instruction remains logistically demanding even for seasoned educators.

words.meaning: học tập qua trải nghiệm thực tế
words.definition: The process of acquiring knowledge and insight through direct practical involvement and structured reflection.
words.example: Fieldwork and industry placements exemplify experiential learning by bridging abstract theory with real-world complexity.

words.meaning: học tập tương trợ cùng bạn đồng trang lứa
words.definition: An educational approach in which students actively support and instruct one another to deepen mutual comprehension.
words.example: Universities increasingly embed peer-assisted learning into first-year modules to reduce attrition and boost confidence.

words.meaning: nhà bác học tinh thông nhiều lĩnh vực
words.definition: An individual possessing profound expertise across multiple distinct fields of knowledge.
words.example: Hyper-specialised degree tracks rarely cultivate the breadth of perspective associated with a classical polymath.

words.meaning: thần đồng, người có tài năng xuất chúng từ sớm
words.definition: A young person endowed with exceptional talent or intellect far beyond their age.
words.example: Accelerating a mathematical prodigy into university lectures without emotional support can inadvertently cause social alienation.

words.meaning: thủ khoa tốt nghiệp đại diện phát biểu
words.definition: The highest-ranking graduating student selected to deliver the farewell address at commencement.
words.example: Although she graduated as class valedictorian, she stressed that collaborative curiosity mattered more than grades.

words.meaning: kỳ nghỉ phép nghiên cứu của giảng viên đại học
words.definition: A period of paid leave granted periodically to university academics for research, writing, or travel.
words.example: During her year-long sabbatical, the professor compiled comparative datasets on bilingual primary schools across Europe.

words.meaning: chế độ biên chế học thuật lâu dài cho giảng viên
words.definition: Permanent academic employment status designed to safeguard scholars' freedom of inquiry and speech.
words.example: Defenders of university tenure contend that job security empowers researchers to pursue unconventional yet vital inquiries.

words.meaning: quỹ hiến tặng lâu dài cho cơ sở giáo dục
words.definition: Financial assets donated to an educational institution to generate ongoing income for scholarships and research.
words.example: Elite institutions with multibillion-dollar endowment funds can weather public funding cuts far better than regional colleges.

words.meaning: học bổng hỗ trợ tài chính theo hoàn cảnh
words.definition: A monetary grant awarded to a student on the basis of financial need to help cover study costs.
words.example: Without a means-tested bursary, many talented applicants from rural districts would be deterred by living expenses.

words.meaning: khoản trợ cấp sinh hoạt định kỳ cho nghiên cứu sinh
words.definition: A fixed regular allowance paid to postgraduate researchers or fellows to cover basic living expenses.
words.example: Unless doctoral stipend levels keep pace with urban rents, academia risks losing promising scholars to corporate jobs.

words.meaning: trường cũ nơi từng theo học và tốt nghiệp
words.definition: The university, college, or school that a person previously attended and graduated from.
words.example: Successful alumni frequently endow laboratories at their alma mater to expand research opportunities for younger cohorts.

words.meaning: buổi tọa đàm, hội thảo học thuật chuyên sâu
words.definition: An academic seminar or formal gathering where specialists present and debate recent research findings.
words.example: Weekly departmental colloquium sessions expose postgraduate students to rigorous questioning from visiting academics.

words.meaning: hội nghị chuyên đề quy tụ các chuyên gia
words.definition: A formal conference at which multiple experts deliver papers and exchange views on a defined subject.
words.example: An international education symposium in Helsinki examined how teacher autonomy correlates with student well-being.

words.meaning: chuyên khảo học thuật sâu về một chủ đề duy nhất
words.definition: A detailed, book-length scholarly study devoted to a single specialised subject.
words.example: Her landmark monograph on early literacy reform reshaped teacher-training curricula across three provinces.

words.meaning: tuyển tập tóm lược toàn diện kiến thức
words.definition: A concise yet comprehensive collection of detailed information on a particular academic subject.
words.example: The ministry published a digital compendium of evidence-based classroom interventions for secondary educators.

words.meaning: kỹ thuật hoặc công cụ hỗ trợ ghi nhớ
words.definition: A structured pattern, acronym, or association used to assist in retaining and recalling information.
words.example: While a clever mnemonic helps medical students recall anatomical sequences, conceptual mastery still requires clinical practice.

words.meaning: tải trọng nhận thức lên trí nhớ làm việc
words.definition: The total amount of mental effort being exerted in working memory during a learning task.
words.example: Cluttered multimedia slides increase extraneous cognitive load and hinder students from absorbing core concepts.

words.meaning: chức năng điều hành nhận thức (lập kế hoạch, tập trung, tự kiểm soát)
words.definition: Higher-order mental skills including planning, impulse control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility.
words.example: Early playful interaction strengthens executive functioning, which predicts long-term academic resilience better than memorisation.

words.definition: An educational philosophy encouraging learners to question power structures, assumptions, and social inequities.
words.example: Advocates of critical pedagogy contend that schooling should cultivate active citizens rather than passive test-takers.

words.meaning: năng khiếu hướng nghiệp, khả năng bẩm sinh về nghề nghiệp
words.definition: Natural inclination or suitability for acquiring specific practical or technical occupational skills.
words.example: Guidance counsellors should evaluate vocational aptitude alongside exam scores so students can pursue fulfilling trades.

words.meaning: chủ nghĩa sùng bái bằng cấp
words.definition: Excessive reliance on formal academic degrees or certificates as the primary measure of competence.
words.example: Growing credentialism has forced entry-level applicants to acquire master's degrees for roles that previously required on-the-job training.

words.meaning: tinh thần ham hiểu biết và khám phá tri thức
words.definition: An intrinsic desire to investigate complex ideas, ask probing questions, and pursue deeper understanding.
words.example: Rigidly scripted syllabuses often extinguish intellectual curiosity before pupils even reach upper secondary school.

words.meaning: thuộc về tri thức luận và bản chất của sự hiểu biết
words.definition: Relating to knowledge, its sources, validity, and the degree of justification behind beliefs.
words.example: University writing courses should foster epistemic humility so students evaluate competing evidence without dogmatism.

words.meaning: thấm nhuần, khắc sâu giá trị hay thói quen thông qua giảng dạy bền bỉ
words.definition: To instil an attitude, ethical principle, or intellectual habit firmly through persistent instruction.
words.example: Primary schools play a pivotal role in helping to inculcate civic empathy and disciplined study habits early in life.

words.meaning: khai sáng, nâng cao trí tuệ và phẩm hạnh
words.definition: To instruct or enlighten someone in a way that improves their intellectual or moral understanding.
words.example: Publicly funded educational documentaries aim to edify broad audiences rather than merely chase commercial ratings.

words.meaning: nhồi sọ, áp đặt tư tưởng một chiều không cho phản biện
words.definition: To teach a person or group to accept a set of beliefs uncritically without tolerating dissent.
words.example: Democratic curricula are explicitly designed to educate citizens in critical inquiry rather than indoctrinate them with dogma.

words.meaning: tình trạng cảnh cáo học vụ
words.definition: A formal warning period during which a student whose grades fall below minimum standards must improve to remain enrolled.
words.example: Universities that pair academic probation with structured mentoring report markedly higher retention rates.

realms.name: The Primordial Wilds
realms.desc: Brave nature, ecology, and climate terminology.

words.definition: the cutting down of large areas of forest
words.example: Large-scale deforestation threatens countless plant and animal species.

words.meaning: dấu chân carbon (lượng khí thải CO₂)
words.definition: the amount of carbon dioxide produced by the activities of a person or organisation
words.example: Cycling to work is a simple way to reduce your carbon footprint.

words.definition: energy from sources that are naturally replaced, such as wind or sunlight
words.example: Governments should offer subsidies to households that switch to renewable energy.

words.definition: fuels such as coal, oil and gas formed from the remains of ancient organisms
words.example: Burning fossil fuels is the main cause of rising greenhouse gas levels.

words.definition: the variety of plants and animals in a particular place
words.example: Coral reefs support an extraordinary level of biodiversity.

words.meaning: loài có nguy cơ tuyệt chủng
words.definition: a type of animal or plant that may soon disappear completely
words.example: Poaching has pushed many endangered species to the edge of extinction.

words.definition: gases sent into the air, especially from vehicles and factories
words.example: Stricter regulations are needed to curb emissions from heavy industry.

words.definition: able to continue for a long time without damaging the environment
words.example: Sustainable farming protects the soil for future generations.

words.definition: the process of something being damaged or made worse
words.example: Overgrazing has led to severe land degradation in some regions.

words.definition: to make something harmful less severe
words.example: Planting trees in cities can help mitigate the effects of heatwaves.

words.definition: a place where waste is buried under the ground
words.example: Most plastic packaging ends up in landfill or in the ocean.

words.definition: plastic items designed to be thrown away after one use
words.example: Several countries have banned single-use plastics such as straws and bags.

words.definition: the protection of the natural environment, plants and animals
words.example: Conservation efforts have helped some whale populations recover.

words.definition: the natural home of an animal or plant
words.example: Habitat loss is one of the greatest threats to wildlife.

words.definition: very severe weather such as floods, droughts or storms
words.example: Extreme weather events are becoming more frequent as the climate warms.

words.definition: a long period with little or no rain
words.example: A prolonged drought can devastate crops and drive up food prices.

words.definition: impossible to change back to a previous state
words.example: Scientists warn that some damage to ecosystems may be irreversible.

words.definition: to treat used materials so that they can be used again
words.example: Local councils should make it easier for residents to recycle household waste.

words.definition: all the living things in an area and the way they affect each other
words.example: Introducing a new species can disrupt a fragile ecosystem.

words.definition: a substance that makes air, water or soil dirty or harmful
words.example: Factories must filter pollutants before releasing waste water into rivers.

words.definition: the gradual increase in the temperature of the earth's atmosphere
words.example: Tackling global warming requires cooperation between all nations.

words.definition: a tax on fuels based on how much carbon dioxide they produce
words.example: A carbon tax would encourage companies to adopt cleaner technologies.

words.definition: a reduction in the amount of something until very little remains
words.example: Overfishing has led to the depletion of fish stocks in many seas.

words.definition: not harmful to the environment
words.example: Consumers are increasingly willing to pay more for eco-friendly products.

words.definition: to make more people know about a problem or issue
words.example: Social media campaigns can raise awareness of environmental issues among young people.

words.definition: caused by human activity
words.example: Most scientists agree that recent warming is largely anthropogenic.

words.definition: the warming of the earth caused by gases trapping heat in the atmosphere
words.example: Methane intensifies the greenhouse effect far more than carbon dioxide in the short term.

words.definition: producing no net carbon emissions
words.example: The company aims to become carbon neutral by 2035.

words.definition: a state in which emissions are balanced by removal from the atmosphere
words.example: Many countries have pledged to reach net zero by 2050.

words.definition: to reduce the carbon emissions of an activity or sector
words.example: Electric trains help decarbonise transport.

words.definition: to capture and store carbon so it does not enter the atmosphere
words.example: Peatlands sequester large amounts of carbon.

words.definition: the impact of a person or community on the environment
words.example: Eating less meat can reduce your ecological footprint.

words.definition: using natural resources faster than they can recover
words.example: Overexploitation has driven some fisheries to collapse.

words.definition: catching so many fish that populations cannot recover
words.example: Overfishing threatens the livelihoods of coastal communities.

words.definition: illegally hunting or catching animals
words.example: Rhino poaching is driven by demand for horn.

words.definition: the death of an entire species
words.example: Many amphibians are on the brink of extinction.

words.meaning: hành lang động vật hoang dã
words.definition: a strip of habitat connecting separate natural areas
words.example: Wildlife corridors allow animals to move safely between forests.

words.definition: restoring land to its natural state and reintroducing species
words.example: Rewilding projects have brought beavers back to parts of Britain.

words.definition: replanting trees where forest has been lost
words.example: Reforestation can restore damaged river catchments.

words.definition: the process by which fertile land becomes desert
words.example: Overgrazing accelerates desertification.

words.definition: the washing or blowing away of the top layer of soil
words.example: Tree roots help prevent soil erosion.

words.definition: a lack of sufficient clean water
words.example: Population growth worsens water scarcity in dry regions.

words.definition: the increase in the average level of the oceans
words.example: Low-lying deltas are threatened by sea-level rise.

words.definition: a period of unusually hot weather
words.example: Prolonged heatwaves put elderly people at risk.

words.definition: a sudden, severe flood
words.example: Heavy rain triggered flash floods in the mountains.

words.definition: an event such as a flood or earthquake that causes great damage
words.example: Coastal regions are particularly prone to natural disasters.

words.meaning: khả năng chống chịu, phục hồi
words.definition: the ability to recover quickly from difficulties or damage
words.example: Mangroves increase the resilience of coastlines to storms.

words.definition: changes made to cope with new conditions
words.example: Sea walls are one form of climate adaptation.

words.definition: to make something impure by adding a harmful substance
words.example: Chemicals from farms can contaminate drinking water.

words.definition: containing poisonous substances capable of causing serious harm or death
words.example: Illegal dumping of toxic waste harms local communities.

words.definition: air pollution mixed with fog
words.example: Thick smog forced schools in the capital to close.

words.definition: tiny particles in the air that damage health
words.example: High levels of particulate matter damage the lungs.

words.definition: rain made acidic by air pollution
words.example: Acid rain damaged forests across Europe in the 1980s.

words.definition: a layer of the atmosphere that blocks harmful ultraviolet rays
words.example: The ban on CFCs has helped the ozone layer recover.

words.definition: able to break down naturally
words.example: Biodegradable packaging reduces plastic pollution.

words.definition: that cannot be replaced once used up
words.example: Oil and coal are non-renewable resources.

words.definition: limited in amount
words.example: Because the planet's fossil fuel reserves are finite, governments must accelerate the transition to renewable energy.

words.definition: producing electricity from moving water
words.example: Hydroelectric dams can displace local communities.

words.definition: electricity produced by nuclear reactions
words.example: Nuclear power produces little carbon but creates radioactive waste.

words.definition: using less energy to perform the same task
words.example: Better insulation improves the energy efficiency of homes.

words.definition: protected land around a city where building is restricted
words.example: Building on the green belt is highly controversial.

words.definition: areas of land covered by shallow water
words.example: Wetlands act as natural flood defences.

words.definition: a tree that grows in coastal salt water
words.example: Mangrove forests protect coastlines from storms.

words.meaning: hiện tượng san hô bị tẩy trắng
words.definition: corals turning white because of heat stress
words.example: Rising sea temperatures cause mass coral bleaching.

words.definition: the falling pH of the oceans as they absorb carbon dioxide
words.example: Ocean acidification makes it harder for shellfish to build shells.

words.definition: a series of organisms in which each is eaten by the next
words.example: Microplastics can enter the food chain through fish.

words.definition: tiny pieces of plastic in the environment
words.example: Microplastics have been found in drinking water.

words.definition: discarded electronic devices
words.example: Much e-waste is shipped to developing countries.

words.definition: turning waste materials into products of higher value
words.example: Upcycling turns old furniture into new designs.

words.definition: an economy that reuses and recycles materials to cut waste
words.example: A circular economy keeps materials in use for as long as possible.

words.definition: a habit of discarding things rather than reusing or repairing them
words.example: Cheap fashion fuels a throwaway culture.

words.definition: cheap clothes produced quickly to follow trends
collocations: the environmental cost of fast fashion
words.example: Fast fashion generates huge amounts of textile waste.

words.meaning: tẩy xanh (quảng cáo xanh giả tạo)
words.definition: misleading claims that a product is environmentally friendly
words.example: Regulators are cracking down on greenwashing.

words.meaning: có ý thức bảo vệ môi trường
words.definition: aware of and concerned about the environment
words.example: Environmentally conscious consumers choose reusable products.

words.meaning: điểm tới hạn (không thể đảo ngược)
words.definition: the point at which a small change causes a large, irreversible effect
words.example: Scientists fear the Amazon rainforest could reach a tipping point.

words.definition: causing great damage or suffering
words.example: Unchecked warming could have catastrophic consequences.

words.definition: to destroy or badly damage something
words.example: The cyclone devastated coastal villages.

words.definition: easily harmed or affected
words.example: Small island nations are especially vulnerable to rising seas.

words.meaning: trách nhiệm gìn giữ môi trường
words.definition: responsible care for the natural environment
words.example: Indigenous communities often practise careful environmental stewardship.

words.meaning: có hiệu lực ràng buộc pháp lý
words.definition: that must be obeyed by law
words.example: Countries signed a legally binding agreement to cut emissions.

words.meaning: mua bán hạn ngạch phát thải
words.definition: a system in which companies buy and sell permits to emit greenhouse gases
words.example: The EU runs an emissions trading scheme for heavy industry.

words.meaning: nguyên tắc người gây ô nhiễm phải trả tiền
words.definition: the principle that those who cause pollution should pay for it
words.example: Under the polluter pays principle, factories fund the clean-up.

words.meaning: đánh giá tác động môi trường
words.definition: a study of how a project will affect the environment
collocations: carry out an environmental impact assessment
words.example: Large infrastructure projects require an environmental impact assessment.

words.definition: a person who works to protect nature
words.example: Conservationists warn that the species could vanish within a decade.

words.definition: tourism that supports conservation and benefits local people
words.example: Eco-tourism can fund the protection of rainforests.

words.definition: an area where wildlife and plants are protected
words.example: The wetland was declared a nature reserve.

words.definition: a non-native species that spreads and harms local wildlife
words.example: Invasive species can wipe out native plants.

words.definition: originating naturally in a particular place
words.example: Indigenous plants are better adapted to local conditions.

words.definition: a chemical used to kill insects that damage crops
words.example: Some pesticides have been linked to declining bee populations.

words.definition: farming without artificial chemicals
words.example: Organic farming avoids synthetic pesticides.

words.definition: growing a single crop over a large area
words.example: Monocultures make crops vulnerable to disease.

words.definition: to fill something up again
words.example: Heavy rains help replenish underground water supplies.

words.definition: water held underground in soil or rock
words.example: Over-pumping has caused groundwater levels to fall.

words.definition: a person forced to leave home because of environmental change
collocations: a growing number of climate refugees
words.example: Rising seas could create millions of climate refugees.

words.definition: to control and use natural forces
words.example: Countries are learning to harness the power of the sun.

words.definition: planting trees where there was no forest before
words.example: Afforestation schemes can help absorb carbon dioxide.

words.definition: a scientist who studies living things and their environment
words.example: Ecologists study how species interact within ecosystems.

words.definition: a city area that is significantly warmer than the countryside around it
words.example: Dark roads and concrete buildings intensify the urban heat island effect.

words.definition: to reduce or stop the effect of something by doing something that works against it
words.example: Regular exercise can help counteract the effects of sitting all day.

words.definition: expected or predicted to happen
words.example: The cooling effect turned out to be larger than anticipated.

words.meaning: sự thoát hơi nước (ở lá cây)
words.definition: the process by which plants release water vapour through their leaves
words.example: Trees cool their surroundings partly through transpiration.

words.definition: the layer of branches and leaves formed by the tops of trees
words.example: Neighbourhoods with more canopy cover stay cooler in summer.

words.definition: increasing rapidly in amount, intensity or seriousness
words.example: Escalating housing costs are pushing young families out of city centres.

words.definition: to balance one effect with an opposite one
words.example: Planting forests can only partly offset carbon emissions.

words.meaning: đầy tham vọng, quy mô lớn
words.definition: needing a lot of effort, money or time to succeed
words.example: The city launched an ambitious programme to plant a million trees.

words.definition: having a mild climate that is neither very hot nor very cold
words.example: Trees grow quickly in temperate regions with regular rainfall.

words.definition: containing a lot of water vapour in the air
words.example: Hot and humid weather makes physical work exhausting.

words.meaning: hiện tượng phú dưỡng nguồn nước gây tảo nở hoa và thiếu oxy
words.definition: Excessive enrichment of water bodies with nutrients, triggering dense algal blooms that deplete dissolved oxygen.
words.example: Unchecked agricultural fertiliser runoff has accelerated eutrophication across coastal estuaries, creating vast marine dead zones.

words.meaning: tầng đất đóng băng vĩnh cửu vùng cực
words.definition: A thick subsurface layer of soil and rock that remains continuously frozen for two or more consecutive years.
words.example: Thawing Arctic permafrost threatens to release billions of tonnes of trapped methane, amplifying global warming feedbacks.

words.meaning: bể hấp thụ và lưu trữ carbon tự nhiên
words.definition: A natural reservoir such as a forest, peatland, or ocean that absorbs more atmospheric carbon than it emits.
words.example: Preserving old-growth tropical rainforests is vital because they operate as an irreplaceable terrestrial carbon sink.

words.meaning: suất phản chiếu bức xạ mặt trời của bề mặt Trái Đất
words.definition: The proportion of incoming solar radiation reflected by a planetary surface, notably high over snow and ice.
words.example: As polar sea ice retreats, lower planetary albedo causes dark ocean water to absorb substantially more solar heat.

words.definition: An underground layer of water-bearing permeable rock or unconsolidated material from which groundwater can be extracted.
words.example: Intensive irrigation in semi-arid farming belts is pumping fossil water far faster than each deep aquifer can recharge.

words.meaning: lưu vực thoát nước, vùng đầu nguồn sông
words.definition: An area of land that drains all streams and rainfall to a common river, basin, or coastal outlet.
words.example: Restoring native vegetation along the upper watershed significantly reduces downstream flooding and sediment siltation.

words.meaning: công nghệ xử lý ô nhiễm bằng vi sinh vật và thực vật
words.definition: The deliberate use of living microorganisms or plants to break down or neutralise hazardous environmental pollutants.
words.example: Following offshore oil spills, coastal authorities increasingly deploy bioremediation to degrade persistent hydrocarbons safely.

words.meaning: hệ thống canh tác nông lâm kết hợp
words.definition: A sustainable land-use system that integrates trees and shrubs with crops or livestock on the same plot.
words.example: Smallholders adopting agroforestry enjoy more stable harvests while simultaneously curbing topsoil erosion and boosting shade.

words.meaning: nông nghiệp bền vững mô phỏng hệ sinh thái tự nhiên
words.definition: An agricultural design philosophy aiming to create self-sustaining ecosystems that mimic natural ecological patterns.
words.example: Community farms built around permaculture principles minimise synthetic inputs by composting organic waste into fertile mulch.

words.meaning: thuộc về địa nhiệt (nhiệt lượng từ lòng đất)
words.definition: Relating to or produced by the internal thermal energy stored beneath the Earth's crust.
words.example: Unlike intermittent wind or solar arrays, geothermal power stations can supply steady baseload electricity around the clock.

words.meaning: thuộc quang điện (chuyển hóa trực tiếp ánh sáng thành điện năng)
words.definition: Relating to the direct conversion of light radiation into electrical current using semiconductor materials.
words.example: Dramatic price drops in photovoltaic panels have made rooftop solar generation economically viable for middle-income households.

words.meaning: nước rỉ rác chứa chất độc hại từ bãi chôn lấp
words.definition: Contaminated liquid that percolates through solid waste in a landfill and extracts dissolved toxic chemicals.
words.example: Modern sanitary landfills must install impermeable clay liners to prevent hazardous leachate from seeping into local rivers.

words.meaning: sự tích tụ sinh học của độc tố trong cơ thể sinh vật
words.definition: The gradual build-up of persistent chemical substances, such as mercury or pesticides, within a living organism over time.
words.example: Marine biologists warn that the bioaccumulation of heavy metals in apex predatory fish poses serious risks to coastal diets.

words.meaning: hiệu ứng dây chuyền qua các bậc dinh dưỡng trong hệ sinh thái
words.definition: Powerful indirect ecological interactions triggered when changes in apex predator populations ripple across lower food-web levels.
words.example: Reintroducing wolves to Yellowstone sparked a remarkable trophic cascade that allowed riverside willow groves to regenerate.

words.meaning: loài chủ chốt duy trì cấu trúc toàn bộ hệ sinh thái
words.definition: An organism whose ecological role has a disproportionately large effect on maintaining the stability of its community.
words.example: Because sea otters restrain kelp-grazing urchins, losing this keystone species can rapidly collapse an entire underwater forest.

words.meaning: sự phân mảnh sinh cảnh tự nhiên
words.definition: The division of large, continuous natural environments into smaller, isolated patches due to roads, farming, or construction.
words.example: Motorways cutting through national parks accelerate habitat fragmentation, restricting gene flow among large mammals.

words.meaning: quá trình diễn thế sinh thái tự nhiên
words.definition: The gradual, predictable sequence of species composition changes as a biological community develops or recovers after disturbance.
words.example: Following a controlled wildfire, ecological succession allows pioneer grasses to stabilise soil before hardwood trees return.

words.meaning: sức chứa sinh thái tối đa của một môi trường
words.definition: The maximum population size or level of resource consumption an environment can sustain indefinitely without degrading.
words.example: Unregulated coastal tourism has pushed several Mediterranean islands well beyond their freshwater carrying capacity.

words.meaning: quá trình nhiễm mặn đất đai và nguồn nước ngọt
words.definition: The accumulation of water-soluble salts in soil or freshwater bodies to levels that impair crop growth and ecosystems.
words.example: Rising sea levels and upstream damming have intensified delta salinisation, threatening rice harvests for millions of farmers.

words.meaning: quá trình khô hạn hóa dài hạn ở quy mô khu vực
words.definition: A long-term climatic shift toward progressively drier conditions that permanently reduces regional water availability.
words.example: Hydrologists distinguish temporary droughts from structural aridification, which demands lasting redesign of municipal water grids.

words.meaning: sự tan lùi và thu hẹp diện tích của sông băng
words.definition: The progressive shrinking of a glacier's terminus when annual ice melt consistently exceeds snowfall accumulation.
words.example: Accelerated glacial retreat across the Himalayas jeopardises dry-season drinking water supplies for densely populated river basins.

words.meaning: sự giãn nở nhiệt của khối nước đại dương
words.definition: The increase in volume of ocean water as it absorbs excess atmospheric heat, contributing directly to sea-level rise.
words.example: Alongside melting polar ice sheets, oceanic thermal expansion accounts for nearly half of observed global sea-level rise.

words.meaning: các giải pháp giảm nhẹ biến đổi khí hậu tại nguồn
words.definition: Deliberate policies and technologies aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions or enhancing carbon removal from the atmosphere.
words.example: Decarbonising heavy industry and electrifying freight fleets remain the twin pillars of credible national climate mitigation.

words.meaning: khả năng chống chịu và phục hồi trước biến đổi khí hậu
words.definition: The capacity of communities, infrastructure, and ecosystems to anticipate, absorb, and recover from extreme climate shocks.
words.example: Constructing sponge-city wetlands and flood-proof transit corridors strengthens urban climate resilience against erratic monsoons.

words.meaning: công tác cải tạo và phục hồi môi trường ô nhiễm
words.definition: The removal or neutralisation of pollutants from contaminated soil, groundwater, or industrial sites to restore ecological safety.
words.example: Before former mining zones can be converted into public parkland, developers must finance rigorous environmental remediation.

words.meaning: điểm nóng đa dạng sinh học đang bị đe dọa nghiêm trọng
words.definition: A biogeographic region that harbours exceptional concentrations of endemic species while facing acute habitat loss.
words.example: International conservation grants increasingly prioritise each tropical biodiversity hotspot where logging threatens undocumented flora.

words.meaning: đặc hữu, chỉ phân bố tự nhiên tại một vùng địa lý nhất định
words.definition: Native to and exclusively restricted to a specific geographical area or isolated ecosystem.
words.example: Invasive predators pose an existential threat to flightless birds that are endemic to remote oceanic islands.

words.meaning: thuộc về tán cây hoặc sinh sống chủ yếu trên cây
words.definition: Living in, inhabiting, or closely associated with trees and forest canopies.
words.example: Building rope bridges across forest clearings allows endangered arboreal primates to forage safely without descending to roads.

words.meaning: thuộc vùng biển khơi xa bờ
words.definition: Relating to the open sea water column away from both the shoreline and the ocean floor.
words.example: Establishing high-seas marine reserves is essential to safeguard migratory pelagic species from industrial drift-net fleets.

words.meaning: thuộc vùng cửa sông giao thoa nước ngọt và nước mặn
words.definition: Relating to or formed in a tidal estuary where freshwater rivers meet and mix with coastal seawater.
words.example: Industrial dredging has degraded fragile estuarine nurseries that juvenile fish rely on before migrating out to sea.

words.meaning: quá trình khử muối biến nước biển thành nước ngọt
words.definition: The industrial process of removing dissolved salts and minerals from seawater to produce potable freshwater.
words.example: While reverse-osmosis desalination secures drinking supplies in arid coastal states, disposing of hypersaline brine remains controversial.

words.meaning: lâm sinh học (khoa học quản lý, trồng mới và tái sinh rừng)
words.definition: The science and practice of controlling the establishment, growth, composition, and ecological health of forests.
words.example: Selective-harvest silviculture balances commercial timber demand with the preservation of multi-layered woodland habitats.

words.meaning: công nghệ thu giữ khí carbon từ nguồn phát thải hoặc không khí
words.definition: The technological process of trapping carbon dioxide emissions at industrial sources or directly from ambient air for storage.
words.example: Energy analysts caution that carbon capture should supplement rapid fossil-fuel phaseouts rather than excuse delayed action.

words.meaning: tình trạng tiêu thụ tài nguyên vượt ngưỡng tái tạo sinh thái
words.definition: A state in which human demand for natural resources and waste absorption exceeds the biosphere's regenerative capacity.
words.example: Shifting away from linear extraction is imperative if humanity intends to reverse decades of global ecological overshoot.

words.meaning: xóa sổ hoàn toàn một loài khỏi một khu vực cụ thể
words.definition: To completely destroy or eliminate a species or population from a particular geographic region.
words.example: Unchecked wetland drainage could extirpate rare amphibian populations from lowland floodplains within a single decade.

words.meaning: tàn phá, khai thác cạn kiệt làm mất vẻ đẹp và tài nguyên thiên nhiên
words.definition: To strip a landscape or ecosystem of its natural resources, beauty, or ecological integrity through reckless exploitation.
words.example: Strict mining moratoriums were enacted to prevent unlicensed corporations from continuing to despoil pristine alpine valleys.

words.meaning: thích nghi dần với điều kiện khí hậu hoặc môi trường mới
words.definition: To adapt physiologically or behaviourally to a new climate, altitude, or altered environmental regime.
words.example: Many cold-water coral reefs simply cannot acclimatise rapidly enough to survive consecutive marine heatwaves.

words.meaning: xét về phương diện sinh thái học
words.definition: In a manner concerning the relationships between living organisms and their surrounding physical environment.
words.example: Monoculture timber plantations may appear green from above yet remain ecologically impoverished compared with native woodlands.

words.meaning: một cách không thể cứu vãn hay phục hồi
words.definition: In a way that makes recovery, reversal, or restoration permanently impossible.
words.example: Once ancient peat bogs are drained and burned, vast stores of millennia-old carbon are irretrievably lost to the sky.

words.meaning: kỷ nguyên Nhân sinh (thời đại hoạt động con người định hình địa chất và khí hậu)
words.definition: The proposed geological epoch characterised by pervasive human dominance over Earth's climate and biophysical systems.
words.example: Environmental historians argue that surviving the anthropocene requires rethinking economic progress within planetary boundaries.

realms.name: The Cyber Foundry
realms.desc: Conquer AI, computing, and technological innovation.

words.definition: the newest and most advanced
words.example: The hospital has invested in cutting-edge diagnostic equipment.

words.definition: computer systems that can do tasks that normally need human intelligence
words.example: Artificial intelligence is already changing how doctors diagnose diseases.

words.definition: the use of machines to do work that was previously done by people
words.example: Automation may replace many routine factory jobs in the coming decade.

words.definition: no longer used because something newer exists
words.example: Smartphones have made many separate devices, such as cameras and maps, almost obsolete.

words.definition: a new idea, method or invention
words.example: Governments can foster innovation by funding research in universities.

words.definition: an important discovery that helps solve a problem
words.example: The new vaccine was hailed as a major medical breakthrough.

words.definition: the gap between people who have access to modern technology and those who do not
words.example: Free public Wi-Fi could help bridge the digital divide between rich and poor.

words.definition: easy for people to use or understand
words.example: The app's user-friendly design makes it popular among older people.

words.definition: the protection of personal information from being misused
words.example: Many users are worried about how technology companies handle data privacy.

words.definition: crime committed using computers or the internet
words.example: Banks are investing heavily to protect customers from cybercrime.

words.definition: time spent using a phone, computer or television
words.example: Parents are advised to limit children's screen time before bed.

words.definition: making you unable to stop doing or using something
words.example: Many apps are deliberately designed to be addictive.

words.definition: the careful watching of people, especially by the police or government
words.example: Facial recognition technology has raised fears of mass surveillance.

words.definition: working from home or from a place outside the office
words.example: Fast internet connections have made remote work possible for millions of people.

words.meaning: thiết bị nhỏ, đồ công nghệ
words.definition: a small, useful machine or device
words.example: Teenagers often feel pressure to own the latest gadgets.

words.definition: to improve a machine or system by adding newer parts
words.example: Companies must regularly upgrade their systems to stay secure.

words.definition: the state of needing something too much
words.example: Our growing dependence on smartphones may weaken our memory.

words.definition: false or inaccurate information that is spread
words.example: Social media platforms are under pressure to combat misinformation.

words.definition: a set of rules that a computer follows to solve a problem
words.example: Recommendation algorithms decide much of what we watch online.

words.definition: the ability to connect to the internet or to other devices
words.example: Rural areas still suffer from poor internet connectivity.

words.definition: to change something completely and improve it
words.example: The internet has revolutionised the way people shop and communicate.

words.definition: designed to reduce the work needed to do something
words.example: Labour-saving appliances such as washing machines freed up time for leisure.

words.definition: knowing a lot about modern technology
words.example: Tech-savvy children often teach their parents how to use new apps.

words.definition: using the internet to hurt, threaten or embarrass someone
words.example: Schools need clear policies to tackle cyberbullying.

words.definition: a disadvantage or problem
words.example: The main drawback of online shopping is that you cannot try products before buying them.

words.meaning: công nghệ đột phá (làm thay đổi cả ngành)
words.definition: an innovation that transforms an industry or market
words.example: Streaming was a disruptive technology for the music industry.

words.definition: using the latest technology
words.example: The laboratory is fitted with state-of-the-art equipment.

words.definition: a type of AI in which computers learn from data
words.example: Machine learning helps banks detect fraudulent transactions.

words.definition: extremely large data sets analysed to reveal patterns
words.example: Retailers use big data to predict consumers' buying habits.

words.definition: everyday objects connected to the internet
collocations: devices in the Internet of Things
connected through the Internet of Things
words.example: The Internet of Things allows home appliances to communicate with each other.

words.definition: storing and processing data on remote servers
words.example: Cloud computing allows small firms to avoid buying expensive servers.

words.definition: the protection of computer systems from attack
words.example: Hospitals must strengthen their cybersecurity.

words.definition: an incident in which private data is stolen or exposed
words.example: A data breach exposed millions of customers' personal details.

words.definition: converting data into a code to keep it secure
words.example: End-to-end encryption protects private messages.

words.definition: the record of a person's online activity
words.example: Teenagers should consider the digital footprint they leave online.

words.definition: receiving more information than one can process
words.example: Constant notifications contribute to information overload.

words.meaning: khả năng duy trì tập trung
words.definition: the length of time someone can concentrate
words.example: Some researchers believe short videos are shortening attention spans.

words.meaning: thời gian tạm ngừng thiết bị số
words.definition: a period without using digital devices
words.example: A weekend digital detox can reduce stress.

words.definition: a person who dislikes or fears new technology
words.example: Many older people describe themselves as technophobes.

words.definition: someone who uses new technology as soon as it appears
words.example: Early adopters often pay high prices for new devices.

words.definition: devices worn on the body, such as smartwatches
words.example: Wearable technology lets people monitor their heart rate.

words.definition: a computer-generated three-dimensional environment
words.example: Virtual reality is used to train surgeons.

words.definition: digital images layered onto the real world
words.example: Augmented reality apps let shoppers see furniture in their own homes.

words.definition: making you feel completely surrounded by an experience
words.example: Museums now offer immersive digital exhibitions.

words.definition: the way a person interacts with a computer or app
words.example: A clear user interface makes apps easier for older people.

words.definition: easy to use without instructions
words.example: Tablets are intuitive enough for young children to use.

words.definition: designing products to stop working or become outdated after a certain time
words.example: Critics accuse phone manufacturers of planned obsolescence.

words.definition: progress in technology
words.example: Rapid technological advancement has transformed healthcare.

words.definition: converting information into digital form
words.example: The digitisation of medical records saves doctors time.

words.definition: the use of digital technology to change how organisations operate
words.example: Banks have undergone a rapid digital transformation.

words.definition: buying and selling goods online
words.example: E-commerce has hit traditional high-street shops hard.

words.definition: a society in which payments are made electronically
words.example: A cashless society may exclude elderly people.

words.definition: a website or app that connects users or sellers
words.example: Online platforms allow small businesses to reach global customers.

words.meaning: tập đoàn công nghệ khổng lồ
words.definition: a very large and powerful technology company
words.example: Governments are trying to regulate the power of tech giants.

words.definition: complete control of a market by one company
words.example: Critics argue that some search engines hold a near monopoly.

words.definition: to make a process operate by machine
words.example: Banks have automated many routine tasks.

words.definition: the science of designing and using robots
words.example: Advances in robotics are transforming car factories.

words.meaning: thiết bị bay không người lái
words.definition: an aircraft with no pilot, controlled remotely
words.example: Drones are used to deliver medicine to remote villages.

words.definition: making solid objects by printing layers of material
words.example: 3D printing can produce custom medical implants.

words.definition: technology that works with extremely small particles
words.example: Nanotechnology could make solar panels more efficient.

words.definition: using physical features such as fingerprints for identification
words.example: Biometric passports store a digital image of the holder.

words.definition: technology that identifies people from their faces
words.example: Facial recognition cameras raise serious privacy concerns.

words.definition: software that responds to spoken commands
words.example: Voice assistants can help elderly people who live alone.

words.meaning: chatbot, trợ lý trò chuyện tự động
words.definition: a computer program that simulates conversation
words.example: Many companies use chatbots to answer basic queries.

words.definition: artificial intelligence that creates text, images or music
words.example: Generative AI raises difficult questions about copyright.

words.definition: unfair outcomes produced by automated systems
words.example: Algorithmic bias can lead to unfair hiring decisions.

words.meaning: sự giám sát của con người
words.definition: people checking and controlling automated decisions
words.example: Medical AI tools still require human oversight.

words.definition: based on the analysis of data
words.example: Data-driven decisions reduce guesswork in business.

words.meaning: tình thế khó xử về đạo đức
words.definition: a situation with no clearly right moral choice
words.example: Self-driving cars pose an ethical dilemma in unavoidable accidents.

words.definition: being responsible for actions and willing to explain them
words.example: There is little accountability for harmful algorithms.

words.definition: to develop faster than something else
words.example: Technology often outpaces the laws that govern it.

words.definition: to change or progress as quickly as something else
collocations: struggle to keep pace with innovation
words.example: Schools struggle to keep pace with technological change.

words.definition: absolutely necessary
words.example: Smartphones have become indispensable for most people.

words.definition: found everywhere
words.example: Smartphones are now ubiquitous, even in rural areas.

words.definition: spreading widely through an area or group
words.example: Technology has a pervasive influence on daily life.

words.definition: advanced and complex
words.example: Criminals use increasingly sophisticated scams.

words.meaning: sự trục trặc; hoạt động sai
words.definition: a failure to work properly
words.example: A software malfunction grounded hundreds of flights.

words.definition: the ability of devices or software to work together
words.example: Compatibility issues prevent some apps from running on older phones.

words.definition: the amount of data that can be transmitted at once
words.example: Video calls require high bandwidth.

words.definition: a high-speed internet connection
words.example: Many rural areas still lack high-speed broadband.

words.meaning: người sinh ra trong thời đại số
words.definition: a person who grew up with digital technology
words.example: Digital natives adapt quickly to new applications.

words.definition: a lack of contact with other people
words.example: Excessive gaming can lead to social isolation.

words.definition: getting pleasure immediately without having to wait
words.example: Social media feeds a culture of instant gratification.

words.definition: to do several things at the same time
words.example: Research suggests people multitask less effectively than they think.

words.definition: able to use computers competently
words.example: Most office jobs require staff to be computer literate.

words.definition: communication over a distance by telephone, internet, etc.
words.example: Telecommunications have shrunk the distance between countries.

words.definition: a device sent into space to orbit the earth
words.example: Satellite imagery helps scientists track deforestation.

words.meaning: bằng sáng chế; cấp bằng sáng chế
words.definition: a legal right to be the only one to make or sell an invention
words.example: The company holds patents on its battery design.

words.definition: ideas and inventions protected by law
words.example: Online piracy undermines intellectual property rights.

words.definition: illegally copying software, films or music
words.example: Online piracy costs the creative industries a great deal of revenue.

words.definition: software whose code anyone may use and modify freely
words.example: Many universities use open-source software to cut costs.

words.definition: a first model of a new product
words.example: Engineers tested a prototype of the new battery.

words.definition: learning by trying different methods until one works
collocations: a process of trial and error
words.example: Many inventions were developed through trial and error.

words.definition: to start selling a product for profit
words.example: Universities often struggle to commercialise their research.

words.definition: to make goods in large quantities
words.example: Cheap mass-produced goods have changed shopping habits.

words.definition: never having happened before
words.example: Information now spreads at an unprecedented speed.

words.definition: increasing more and more rapidly
words.example: Computing power has seen exponential growth.

words.definition: options that control who can see your data
words.example: Users should review their privacy settings regularly.

words.definition: being unidentified when using the internet
words.example: Online anonymity can encourage abusive behaviour.

words.definition: the networks and systems that support digital services
words.example: Reliable digital infrastructure is vital for remote learning.

words.definition: ideas or guesses about something without firm evidence
words.example: There has been much speculation about the future of work.

words.definition: reliable information based on careful measurement
words.example: Policy decisions should be based on solid data rather than fear.

words.definition: large in size, value or importance
words.example: The policy had a substantial impact on youth unemployment.

words.definition: a person who expects bad things to happen
words.example: Pessimists argue that robots will take most jobs.

words.definition: happening or existing in many places or among many people
words.example: Smartphone use is widespread among teenagers.

words.definition: something that does not happen or exist very often
words.example: Jobs for life are now something of a rarity.

words.meaning: bức tranh tại một thời điểm
words.definition: information that shows what a situation is like at one particular time
words.example: The census provides a snapshot of the population every ten years.

words.meaning: tự chọn tham gia (không ngẫu nhiên)
words.definition: chosen by the participants themselves rather than at random, which may bias results
words.example: Online polls often rely on a self-selected sample.

words.definition: to cause someone or something to be in a particular state
words.example: New technology may render some skills obsolete.

words.definition: the series of steps by which you move to more senior jobs
collocations: the first rung of the career ladder
words.example: Internships help graduates get onto the first rung of the career ladder.

words.meaning: khả năng tương tác và liên thông dữ liệu giữa các hệ thống khác nhau
words.definition: The capability of distinct computer systems, platforms, or devices to exchange and interpret data seamlessly.
words.example: Mandating technical interoperability between competing messaging platforms prevents dominant firms from locking users inside closed ecosystems.

words.meaning: độ trễ truyền dẫn tín hiệu hoặc phản hồi của hệ thống mạng
words.definition: The time delay between initiating a digital instruction or data transmission and receiving the corresponding response.
words.example: Ultra-low network latency is indispensable for remote robotic surgery, where even a split-second lag could endanger patients.

words.meaning: khả năng mở rộng quy mô hệ thống mà vẫn giữ nguyên hiệu suất
words.definition: The capacity of a software architecture or technological system to handle growing workloads efficiently without performance loss.
words.example: Cloud-native infrastructures provide remarkable scalability, enabling public agencies to absorb sudden surges in online tax filings.

words.meaning: mật mã học bảo mật thông tin số
words.definition: The mathematical science of encoding and decoding information to guarantee secure communication and verify authenticity.
words.example: Advances in post-quantum cryptography are urgently needed to ensure banking networks remain impervious to next-generation decryption.

words.meaning: phi tập trung, phân tán quyền kiểm soát trên nhiều nút mạng
words.definition: Distributed across multiple independent nodes rather than controlled by a single central authority or server.
words.example: Proponents argue that decentralised digital registries reduce single points of failure and strengthen resilience against cyberattacks.

words.meaning: công nghệ chuỗi khối lưu trữ sổ cái minh bạch bất biến
words.definition: A cryptographically linked, distributed digital ledger that records transactions transparently across a peer-to-peer network.
words.example: Beyond cryptocurrency, supply-chain auditors are trialling blockchain to verify the ethical provenance of exported raw materials.

words.meaning: mạng nơ-ron nhân tạo mô phỏng cơ chế học của não bộ
words.definition: A computational machine-learning architecture composed of interconnected nodes modelled loosely on biological brain pathways.
words.example: Trained on millions of satellite photographs, the neural network detected illegal logging clearings with unprecedented accuracy.

words.meaning: video hoặc âm thanh giả mạo tinh vi tạo bằng trí tuệ nhân tạo
words.definition: Synthetic video, audio, or imagery generated by deep learning to convincingly depict events or speech that never occurred.
words.example: Electoral regulators warn that a convincing deepfake released hours before polling day could severely distort voter trust.

words.meaning: mã độc tống tiền khóa dữ liệu hệ thống để đòi chuộc
words.definition: Malicious software that encrypts an organisation's vital files and demands monetary payment to restore access.
words.example: A coordinated ransomware intrusion forced several municipal hospitals to revert to paper records for nearly two weeks.

words.meaning: hành vi lừa đảo giả mạo nhằm đánh cắp thông tin nhạy cảm
words.definition: The fraudulent practice of sending deceptive electronic messages disguised as reputable institutions to steal credentials.
words.example: Even sophisticated corporate firewalls remain vulnerable when employees fall prey to highly personalised spear phishing campaigns.

words.meaning: phần mềm độc hại xâm nhập và phá hoại hệ thống máy tính
words.definition: Any software intentionally crafted to disrupt, damage, spy upon, or gain unauthorised control over computer systems.
words.example: Routine software patching remains the single most cost-effective defence against intrusive malware targeting public infrastructure.

words.meaning: lỗ hổng bảo mật mới phát hiện chưa có bản vá chính thức
words.definition: A previously unknown software security flaw that attackers can exploit before developers release a corrective patch.
words.example: National cybersecurity agencies collaborate with ethical hackers to identify any zero-day vulnerability before hostile actors weaponise it.

words.meaning: xác thực danh tính bằng đặc điểm sinh trắc học
words.definition: Security verification that confirms an individual's identity using unique biological traits such as fingerprints or iris patterns.
words.example: While biometric authentication streamlines mobile banking logins, compromised physiological data cannot simply be reset like passwords.

words.meaning: điện toán biên xử lý dữ liệu trực tiếp gần nguồn phát sinh
words.definition: A distributed computing paradigm that processes data close to the physical devices generating it rather than in distant data centres.
words.example: Autonomous factory robots rely on edge computing to analyse sensor feeds instantaneously without saturating central bandwidth.

words.meaning: bản sao số mô phỏng theo thời gian thực một đối tượng vật lý
words.definition: A dynamic virtual replica of a physical object, building, or urban system continuously updated with live sensor data.
words.example: Civil engineers construct a digital twin of an ageing bridge to simulate extreme wind loads before approving structural repairs.
